title: 🔬 Mystery Lab Detective
description: A real lab. A real mystery. You are the scientist. Five plants are dying in the school greenhouse and nobody knows why. Use the scientific method — observe, hypothesize, experiment, analyze, conclude — to crack the case.
subject: science
how_to_play: Read each lab situation carefully — observation is everything.
Form a hypothesis BEFORE you experiment.
Pick the choice that tests ONE variable at a time.
Use evidence to update or reject your hypothesis.
Reach a conclusion supported by your data — not by gut feel.
Bonus: spot when your control group matters.
learning_objectives: Apply the 5 steps of the scientific method to a real problem.
Design experiments that isolate ONE variable (control vs experiment).
Reject hypotheses when evidence contradicts them — without ego.
Recognize when more data is needed before concluding.
cultural_context: School science lab investigation, scientific temper, evidence-based reasoning — core NEP 2020 competencies for middle school.

tick_rules: Each round = 1 day in the lab

rounds.situation: Ms. Aiyer hands you a clipboard. 'Five tomato plants in the greenhouse are dying. Same variety, same age. The other ten are fine. Find out why.' Five sad plants on Bench 3. The others on Bench 4 and 5 look great. The greenhouse hums with cooling fans. What's your FIRST move?
rounds.goal: Begin with the right scientific habit.
rounds.coaching_moment: The first step of science is OBSERVATION — not guessing. Look before you leap.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do scientists observe before they hypothesize?
rounds.image_prompt: Bright school greenhouse, two benches with healthy green tomato plants, one bench with five wilting yellowed tomato plants, student with clipboard observing, semi-realistic warm light

choices.label: A. Guess immediately: 'It's the water — over-watered probably.' Move on.
choices.outcome_text: Ms. Aiyer raises an eyebrow. 'How do you know?' You don't. Step back.

choices.label: B. Carefully observe BOTH benches: leaves, soil, light, position, smell, anything unusual.
choices.learning_concept: Observation is step 1 of the scientific method.
choices.outcome_text: Notes: sick plants are closer to the air-conditioning vent. Their soil is dry on top but waterlogged below. Healthy plants are 2 metres away. INTERESTING.

choices.label: C. Pull up the leaves of the sick plants to inspect roots immediately.
choices.outcome_text: You damage roots before you've fully observed. Now you can't compare roots cleanly. Lesson: observe BEFORE intervening.

choices.label: D. Ask the gardener what they think.
choices.outcome_text: The gardener says 'too much water'. Maybe true, maybe not — but you haven't checked yourself yet. Authority isn't evidence.

scene_widget.caption: Tap plants and adjust the conditions to spot what's different.

rounds.situation: Your observation notes: sick plants near AC vent, soil waterlogged underneath, leaves yellowing from edges. Time to form a HYPOTHESIS — a specific, testable claim. Which is the BEST hypothesis to start with?
rounds.goal: Form a hypothesis that's specific and testable.
rounds.coaching_moment: A good hypothesis is SPECIFIC, TESTABLE, and FALSIFIABLE. 'Plants are sad' isn't a hypothesis. 'Cold air from AC vent is damaging plant cells' is.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why must a hypothesis be 'falsifiable' (provably wrong)?
rounds.image_prompt: Student writing hypothesis in lab notebook, magnifying glass and tomato plant on desk, scientific notes visible, semi-realistic lighting

choices.label: A. 'The plants are sick because they are unhappy.'
choices.outcome_text: Not testable. How would you measure 'happiness'? Move on.

choices.label: B. 'Cold air from the AC vent is causing root damage in plants closer to the vent.'
choices.outcome_text: Excellent. Specific cause (cold air), specific effect (root damage), specific population (vent-side plants). Now you can test it.

choices.label: C. 'Something is wrong with the greenhouse.'
choices.outcome_text: True but useless. Narrow it down.

choices.label: D. 'The plants are dying because of bad luck.'
choices.learning_concept: Bad luck is not a scientific cause.
choices.outcome_text: Science doesn't accept 'bad luck'. There's always a cause — find it.

scene_widget.caption: Drag the temperature slider down on one plant. What changes?

rounds.situation: Hypothesis: cold air from the AC vent is hurting the plants. Now design an experiment. Your teacher has 20 healthy seedlings ready. How do you test this?
rounds.goal: Design an experiment with a control group and ONE variable.
rounds.coaching_moment: A great experiment changes ONE variable and keeps everything else the same. That's the only way you can blame the variable for the result.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do you need a control group?
rounds.image_prompt: Two groups of tomato seedlings in lab trays, one labeled control, one labeled experiment, neat labels, scientific lab setting

choices.label: A. Put 10 plants near AC vent. Leave 10 away from vent. Same soil, water, light. Compare after 7 days.
choices.outcome_text: Textbook design: ONE variable changed (vent exposure), everything else identical. You'll know the cause if results differ.

choices.label: B. Put 10 near vent with cold water, 10 away from vent with warm water. Compare.
choices.outcome_text: You changed TWO things at once (vent + water temp). If results differ, you won't know which caused it.

choices.label: C. Put all 20 plants near the vent. See how many die.
choices.outcome_text: No control = no way to know if the vent is the cause or if plants would die anyway.

choices.label: D. Put 1 plant near vent and 1 plant away from vent. Compare.
choices.outcome_text: Sample of 1 vs 1 is way too small. One sick seedling could be coincidence. Need a bigger N.

props.label: Set up your control + experimental groups

scene_widget.caption: Build two trays — change ONE variable between them.

rounds.situation: Your experiment is running. Day 4: 3 vent-side plants are starting to yellow. Day 5: classmate Pavan offers to 'help' — he wants to move the vent-side plants closer to a heat source 'to balance things out'. What do you do?
rounds.coaching_moment: You don't change conditions mid-experiment. If you do, you ruin your data — and have to start over.
rounds.image_prompt: Lab setting with classmate trying to move a plant to a heat lamp, main scientist holding up hand to stop, scientific lab integrity scene, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. 'No — if we change conditions, our data is contaminated. Wait until Day 7.'
choices.outcome_text: Pavan grumbles, but the experiment continues clean. By Day 7 you have real, defensible data.

choices.label: B. 'Sure, save them — they're suffering.'
choices.learning_concept: Compassion ≠ science. (You'd save them in a real garden, but not in a controlled experiment.)
choices.outcome_text: The experiment is now contaminated. You can't blame the vent — Pavan added heat. Start over.

choices.label: C. 'Move HALF the vent-side plants to heat — that gives a third group.'
choices.outcome_text: Now you have 3 groups but you redesigned the experiment in the middle. Whatever happens, you can't cleanly attribute it.

choices.label: D. 'Run two parallel experiments at once — keep this one and start a heat-lamp one.'
choices.learning_concept: Doable but premature — finish the first one cleanly first.
choices.outcome_text: Decent instinct, but you don't have enough plants/time. Finish what you started.

scene_widget.caption: Step through days. Record what happens at each tick.

rounds.situation: Day 7 results are in. Vent-side group: 7/10 plants yellowing or dying. Away-from-vent group: 1/10 yellowing. Your hypothesis (cold air from vent damages plants) seems supported. But — what does GOOD analysis demand?
rounds.coaching_moment: Strong data ≠ proof. It's *evidence supporting* a hypothesis. The honest scientist also asks 'what could I be missing?'
rounds.reflection_prompt: What's the difference between 'strong evidence' and 'proof'?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab notebook with data table comparing two plant groups, charts showing wilted vs healthy plants, magnifying glass, scientific analysis scene, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. 'Hypothesis is PROVEN. AC vent kills plants. Done.'
choices.outcome_text: Overclaiming. 'Proven' is a word science avoids. Replace with 'evidence supports the hypothesis'.

choices.label: B. 'Strong evidence supports the hypothesis. But: could anything else explain this — like vibration, light differences, or coincidence?'
choices.outcome_text: Excellent thinking. You note the vent area also gets less sunlight and more vibration. Worth flagging in the report.

choices.label: C. 'The hypothesis is wrong because 3 vent-side plants survived.'
choices.learning_concept: Strong tendencies are still real even with exceptions.
choices.outcome_text: Survivors don't disprove a hypothesis. 7/10 vs 1/10 is a strong signal. Look at proportions, not exceptions.

choices.label: D. 'Inconclusive. Run for another month.'
choices.outcome_text: Some caution is good. Endless caution is procrastination. Strong evidence already exists.

scene_widget.caption: Drop your data points. Look for a pattern (or lack of one).

rounds.situation: Your conclusion: cold air from AC vent likely damages tomato seedlings. Pavan asks: 'Should we tell the school to move the vent now?' Ms. Aiyer reminds you: 'A single experiment isn't enough for science.' What's the best next step?
rounds.coaching_moment: One experiment is a hint. Two consistent experiments are evidence. Many consistent experiments approach truth.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is replication the heart of science?
rounds.image_prompt: Multiple lab teams running similar plant experiments, scientists comparing results, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Run the experiment AGAIN with a fresh batch of plants. If results match, confidence grows.
choices.outcome_text: Right answer. Replication catches lucky flukes. Real science is repeated, not just done once.

choices.label: B. Tell the school immediately — move the vent.
choices.learning_concept: Acting on one study can mislead policy.
choices.outcome_text: You COULD recommend a temporary fix, but replication first builds confidence.

choices.label: C. Test a totally different hypothesis next.
choices.learning_concept: Don't abandon a finding before confirming it.
choices.outcome_text: Curious, but premature. Confirm before you move on.

choices.label: D. Publish the findings online and let people debate.
choices.outcome_text: One unreplicated study isn't ready to publish. (This is exactly how bad science spreads.)

scene_widget.caption: Run the trial again with the same setup. Same result?

rounds.situation: Two replications later, the pattern holds: vent-side plants suffer. Ms. Aiyer asks for a one-page report for the principal. How do you write it?
rounds.coaching_moment: Honest scientific communication includes the FINDINGS, the LIMITATIONS, and what's STILL UNKNOWN.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do good scientists state their limitations openly?
rounds.image_prompt: Student finalizing scientific report on laptop, lab data charts on screen, neat handwritten title 'Findings & Limitations', semi-realistic

choices.label: A. 'AC vent is killing the plants. Move it immediately. Case closed.'
choices.outcome_text: Strong-sounding, but unscientific. 'Killing' is dramatic; 'case closed' is overclaim.

choices.label: B. 'Across 3 trials, vent-side plants showed 70%+ damage vs 10% in the control. Likely cause: cold airflow. Limitation: light differences not fully controlled. Recommend: relocate vent OR run a controlled-light follow-up.'
choices.outcome_text: Beautifully written. Clear finding, honest limitations, concrete next step. The principal acts.

choices.label: C. 'Inconclusive — too many factors to be sure.'
choices.learning_concept: Don't bury a strong signal in fake humility.
choices.outcome_text: Excessive caution is its own dishonesty. Three replications with strong effects ≠ inconclusive.

choices.label: D. Long, jargon-heavy report nobody will read.
choices.outcome_text: Real scientists write so the audience UNDERSTANDS. Jargon is laziness.

props.label: Sketch your final lab report figure

scene_widget.caption: Draw the setup so another scientist could replicate it.

rounds.situation: The principal reads your report. The vent gets relocated. Two weeks later, every plant on Bench 3 is healthy. Ms. Aiyer hands you a small card: 'Junior Scientist of the Term.' But — there's a final question. Looking back, what was the SINGLE most important thing you did?
rounds.goal: Reflect on the deepest scientific habit.
rounds.coaching_moment: The greatest scientific skill isn't intelligence — it's the willingness to be wrong AND change your mind based on evidence.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What scientific habit will you carry into non-science life?
rounds.image_prompt: Healthy thriving tomato plants on bench, smiling student receiving certificate, sunny greenhouse scene, semi-realistic warm light

choices.label: A. I had a great hypothesis from the start.
choices.learning_concept: The hypothesis was a STEP, not the win.
choices.outcome_text: Hypotheses are dime a dozen. The work to TEST them is what matters.

choices.label: B. I observed carefully before guessing, designed a clean experiment, and stayed open to being wrong.
choices.learning_concept: The combo of careful observation + clean design + open mind = scientific thinking.
choices.outcome_text: EXACTLY. That's the scientific method in one sentence. You'll use it your whole life — even when you're not in a lab.

choices.label: C. I trusted my gut.
choices.outcome_text: Your gut said 'water'. The data said 'vent'. Gut is starting point, not endpoint.

choices.label: D. I worked hard.
choices.outcome_text: True but generic. Hard work *with* method beats hard work alone.

scene_widget.caption: Now zoom out — see how AC, plants, soil, and light interact.

achievements.title: Hypothesis Crafter
achievements.criteria: Form a specific testable hypothesis in Round 2.

achievements.title: Clean Experiment
achievements.criteria: Design single-variable experiment with control in Round 3.

achievements.title: Lab Integrity
achievements.criteria: Refuse to contaminate experiment in Round 4.

glossary_terms.definition: A specific, testable claim about cause and effect.
The unchanged comparison group in an experiment.
Anything that can change in an experiment. Good experiments change ONE.
Repeating an experiment to confirm results aren't a fluke.
A claim that can be PROVEN WRONG by evidence — required for science.
Recording what's actually there before guessing why.
How many subjects in your study — bigger is more reliable.
An extra variable you didn't notice that's secretly affecting your results.

endings.title: Junior Scientist of the Term
endings.message: You used the scientific method like a pro. Carry this habit into every part of your life.

endings.title: Promising Investigator
endings.message: Solid work. A few wrong turns, but you got there. That's how real science feels.

endings.title: Apprentice Scientist
endings.message: You're learning. Re-run the lab and pay close attention to OBSERVATION → HYPOTHESIS → SINGLE-VARIABLE EXPERIMENT.

checkpoints.prompt: What would have happened if you'd let Pavan move the plants?
Why do scientists state their limitations openly?

reflection_prompt: Which lever, if you'd moved it earlier, would have changed your outcome the most?
